 Cop31 Cop31 as it happened: draft climate deal calls for faster shift away from fossil fuels
 ‘Cancer of indifference’ to climate crisis is pushing the world closer to the brink, says Mia Mottley as UN talks enter second week
  Updated  26m ago Ajit Niranjan Mon 16 Nov 2026 10.27 EST First published on Mon 16 Nov 2026 02.28 EST Share Key events 2m ago Day 8 of Cop31 - recapped 
 3h ago 'Cancer of indifference' to climate crisis pushing world closer to brink - Barbados PM 
 4h ago Draft deal calls for 'accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels' 
 7h ago 'Just transition' under threat, campaigners warn 
 8h ago Deep divides as second week of talks begin 
 Greenpeace activists unveil a three-dimensional floor installation titled ‘Don’t Fall for Fossil Fuels’ at Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey. Photograph: Murad Sezer/Reuters View image in fullscreen Greenpeace activists unveil a three-dimensional floor installation titled ‘Don’t Fall for Fossil Fuels’ at Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey. Photograph: Murad Sezer/Reuters Ajit Niranjan Mon 16 Nov 2026 10.27 EST First published on Mon 16 Nov 2026 02.28 EST Share From 2m ago 10.27 EST Day 8 of Cop31 - recapped
 That’s all for today. Here are the highlights from the eighth day of the 31st UN climate summit:
 Campaigners warned a ‘ just transition ’ was under threat
 The Australian prime minister apologised on Friday after puerile chat with the president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, was caught on camera
 A draft cover text called for ‘ accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels ’, including an ‘immediate’ transition away from them in energy systems
 Some observers expressed scepticism that the hosts had a plan to get such language into the final text
 Barbados prime minister Mia Mottley warned that a “ cancer of indifference ” to the climate crisis is pushing the world closer to the brink
 Delegates danced with rainbow flags in protest against the Turkish government’s crackdown on LGBTQ+ people
 Thanks for following – we’ll be back tomorrow with more.

 26m ago 10.03 EST Damien Gayle UN climate summit delegates danced with rainbow flags on Monday afternoon in a protest against the Turkish government’s crackdown on LGBTQ+ people ahead of Cop31 .
 In the lead up to the talks, police in Turkey arrested dozens in a series of raids of organisations that campaign for LGBTQ rights and support people with HIV, and crackdowns on Pride protests.
 Since mid-September, more than 80 people are reported to have been in pretrial detention. Many face charges related to “obscenity” and alleged violations of the Law on Associations.
 View image in fullscreen LGBTQ+ activists at a protest at Cop31 in Turkey. Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPA In a choreographed piece of political theatre in the Cop31 blue zone, individuals were led with their mouths covered behind a stage prop cell door while the stories of detained LGBTQ+ people were read aloud. Afterwards they danced to one of Turkey’s most-famous gay anthems, which featured two men dancing together in its music video, and whose singer was jailed.
 The protest was organised by members the Women and Gender Constituency, one of nine stakeholder groups formally recognised by the UNFCCC. Turkey’s targeting of LGBTQ+ activists was “outrageous political violence”, said Sinéad Magner, an organiser with WGC.
 “There are certain governments who wish we were invisible, that we pretend we don’t exist. Today, we sent a message to every person sitting today in a cell in Turkey for the crime of existing as themselves: you are not invisible to us. We see you. We stand with you.”
 View image in fullscreen LGBTQ+ activists at a protest at Cop31. Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPA WGC said it called on the Turkish and Australian teams co-hosting this year’s Cop and the UNFCCC secretariat to demand the immediate release “of everyone detained for their human rights and association work”, and to offer a “public, unambiguous guarantee of safety to all COP31 participants”.
 The protest came after climate activists formed a protective ring around Turkish LGBTQ+ activists as they were giving a leading role at the Cop’s annual people’s march on Saturday .
 “Today civil society brought joy to the Cop space at a time of repression and criminalisation for human rights defenders fighting for equality outside these conference walls,” Alexis Deswaef, president of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), said.
 “Climate breakdown is an amplifier of systemic inequalities, including those faced by LGBTQIA+ people. A shrinking civic space for their voices and organisations across the world is sidelining their rights and contributions to climate policies and the fulfilment of all human rights.”
 Share 44m ago 09.46 EST Joe Pinner ‘Climate change is changing the experience of living in the city I call home’ 
 Over the last week I’ve been speaking to young climate activists at Cop31 . Today I spoke to Zainab Bie , 23, from India, who campaigns for practical climate solutions for those living in the global south.
 She is at Cop as a spokesperson for the Children and Youth Pavilion, a youth-led climate action group.
 View image in fullscreen Zainab Bie, 23, from India, is at Cop31 as a spokesperson for the Children and Youth Pavilion. Photograph: Marie Jacquemin/YOUNGO “For much of the year, Delhi can feel like a city you cannot comfortably breathe in. I have grown up watching its summers become more punishing, its heatwaves last longer and its monsoons become harder to predict. Climate change is changing the experience of living in the city I call home.
 “But the consequences are profoundly unequal. While some can retreat indoors, buy clean air or recover from extreme weather, millions of people in India cannot afford to stop working when temperatures become dangerous. A lost day of wages, a damaged home or a failed harvest can push a family further into insecurity. The climate crisis does not affect everyone equally, because the resources to survive it are not equally distributed.
 “Countries like mine deserve accessible, predictable, grant-based climate finance that allows them to protect their lives and livelihoods without taking on more debt. Adaptation finance can no longer remain a promise that governments pass between negotiating rooms. Developing countries need it now. Yet negotiations still risk treating it as part of a broad climate finance pool, without a dedicated delivery plan, clear milestones or accountability.
 “My hope is that Cop31 becomes the Cop that changes the trajectory of our planet. I want a future in which where you are born does not determine how exposed you are to climate disasters, or how much debt your country must take on to protect its people. Climate finance must redistribute resources and power, not reproduce the inequalities that created this crisis.”
 Share 55m ago 09.34 EST If you need a refresher on who the main players are at Cop31 , and what’s at stake in these negotiations, my colleague Fiona Harvey has broken it down here.
 Who’s who at Cop31: key players at the climate talks Read more Cop31: what is at stake at the UN climate summit and what can it achieve? Read more Share 1h ago 09.21 EST Damien Gayle Many civil society campaigners say the early publication of such a long, complicated and apparently contradictory draft cover decision is an attempt to draw attention from deep divisions in negotiations at Cop31 .
 Currently sides are far from agreement in discussion over the climate finance work programme, the Just Transition Mechanism and the global goal on adaptation. Disputes are threatening to derail the entire summit, with some countries refusing to back any cover decision at all until progress is made.
 “We shouldn’t get hung up on the cover text,” said Devina Shah, advocacy manager at Youth and Environment Europe. “It’s a bit of a distraction.”
 Asad Rehman, chief executive of Friends of the Earth, said the cover text was a “mish-mash of contradictory proposals that stand little chance of making it into the final outcome”.
 Leon Sealey-Huggins, senior climate justice campaigner at War On Want, added: “so much energy, attention and time going into the cover decision sucks capacity away from a lot of the other negotiating rooms and issues.
 “Crucially, we are seeing this affect the Just Transition negotiations with the Australian presidency completely dropping the ball on the potential ambition of what should be a crucial enabler of all of the actions necessary to address climate breakdown.”
 Share 2h ago 08.46 EST Gabrielle Canon While the US remains officially on the sidelines in Antalya thanks to Donald Trump’s retreat from international climate agreements over the last two years, it may not stay that way for long.
 At least that’s what representatives from the Democratic Party, fresh from a decisive victory in the midterm elections, pledged on Monday.
 “America is not only back – we are all in,” California Congressman Jared Huffman told reporters, noting that Democrats would soon hold the strongest majority seen in 50 years and would be able to challenge Trump’s anti-climate agenda. “The temporarily empty chair of the United States Cop31 does not represent what the American people and businesses want or need.”
 View image in fullscreen US representative Jared Huffman speaks during the US Congressional delegation press conference at the America Is All In pavilion at the Cop31 summit. Photograph: Chris McGrath/Getty Images Huffman is one of roughly 120 US delegates in attendance at Cop31 – a mix of Congressional lawmakers, governors, and local leaders. They have maintained a US presence and championed climate progress at the talks, despite the president’s “Drill Baby Drill” call to arms, and push for more fossil fuels extraction, deregulation, and a crackdown on climate science.
 “While the Trump administration has shamefully abandoned international climate agreements and attacked climate and clean energy policies, state and federal climate leaders from the United States are here to show the world that they are committed to working with the global community to solve this urgent shared challenge,” said Rachel Cleetus, Climate Program Director for the Union of Concerned Scientists.
 Delegates pointed to work at the subnational level, to advance renewable energy and curb emissions, as a path forward for the world’s second biggest emitter to make progress regardless of who is in the White House. Over the next decade, US state-level policies, market forces, and falling technology costs are positioned to reduce carbon emissions up to 46% below 2005 levels, according to a new analysis from the University of Maryland Center for Global Sustainability and the America Is All In group that backed the delegation.
 That doesn’t mean they aren’t hopeful for a president who would officially reenter the talks. But either way, Huffman said, next year will be different thanks to the landslide victory US voters recently handed to Democrats.
 “We will be an official Congressional delegation led by the leadership of the House of Representatives,” Huffman said. “Soon after that, this yellow part of our lanyard that says ‘observer’ will change – the United States will officially be back in as part of the negotiating effort at a future Cop.”
 Share Updated at  08.47 EST 2h ago 08.18 EST In an editorial published yesterday evening, the Guardian urged negotiators not to derail the green transition. It argues that those pushing for a faster shift away from fossil fuels “are on the side of the future, while their opponents are stuck in the past”. 
 The Cop31 climate talks have acquired something their delegates scarcely expected: a little political breathing space. The comeback by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the second round of Brazil’s presidential race was important for many reasons. Victory for his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, would have marked a dangerous retreat from democracy. But Mr Bolsonaro’s commitment to environmental deregulation would also have spelled disaster for the Amazon, making Lula’s re-election a big win for the climate. Similarly, success by Democrats in the US midterms means that Donald Trump’s destructive grip has been loosened. If they win back the White House in 2028, the US should rejoin the UN process in time for Cop34.
 While the diplomatic picture is less bleak than it might have been, the threat level remains high and rising. António Guterres used his last Cop as UN secretary general to issue a pithy warning that “ it’s make or bake time ”. With the latest analysis pointing to heating of 2.7C by the end of the century – far beyond the 1.5C target in the Paris agreement – governments face another crunch moment: by pivoting away from fossil fuels, they can still avert the most dangerous impacts. Yet the UK’s Andy Burnham was the only G7 leader to make the trip to Turkey; the French and German leaders chose to attend an EU summit in Dublin instead.
 The Guardian view on Cop31: the green transition must not be derailed | Editorial Read more Share 3h ago 07.39 EST 'Cancer of indifference' to climate crisis pushing world closer to brink - Barbados PM
 Fiona Harvey Staying silent on the climate crisis is pushing the world closer to disaster, the prime minister of Barbados , Mia Mottley, has said, urging people around the world to force a confrontation with politicians who are failing to do what is needed.
 Taking action on methane emissions could be the emergency brake that gives the world time to decarbonise, Mottley said. She is urging people to sign a global petition to cut the powerful greenhouse gas .
 She hopes to gather 1.5bn responses to her petition , in an echo of the 1.5C temperature limit countries have pledged to protect. “We have to let them know the good news: that if we can control methane, we can reduce temperature [rises] by 0.3C to 0.5C ,” she said during an interview at the Cop31 UN climate summit , which is taking place in Antalya, Turkey. “We can buy time to continue decarbonising.”
 View image in fullscreen Mia Mottley, prime minister of Barbados, speaking at Cop31 last week. Photograph: Khalil Hamra/AP Mottley, a charismatic leader who has challenged former colonial powers over slavery reparations, gained global recognition five years ago when she criticised rich countries for failing poor and vulnerable people on the climate crisis.
 “Ordinary people have to be able to say what their view is with respect to living on this Earth,” she said. “I hope that by calling on ordinary people to speak out where leaders have failed to lead, we can see the kind of momentum that will cause all of us to reflect on what we’re doing as countries, and prioritise – in ways that do not compromise other aspects of our development – the efforts that are needed [on the climate].”
 The “cancer of indifference” to the climate crisis, she said, would push the world closer to the brink. “We need to break [the climate crisis] down into ordinary simple language, so people understand what is at stake, either by their silence, their inaction, or indeed by their actions.
 Barbados PM urges global citizens to demand methane cuts at Cop31 summit Read more Share 3h ago 07.30 EST Damien Gayle The Cop31 presidency is “treading a dangerous line” with a draft cover text that pushes the “false solution” of carbon dioxide removal and debt-based private climate finance, civil society campaigners have said.
 “Climate action roadmaps without climate finance lead nowhere,” said Siphesihle Hopewell Mvundla of groundWork. “The Global South is spending 225 times more repaying debt than they receive in climate finance from the very countries who owe them a climate debt.”
 The draft text includes a push for carbon dioxide removal as a key part of reversing the overshoot in global heating past 1.5C, saying it “welcomes” the “deployment of Carbon Capture Utilization and Storage and Carbon Dioxide Removal technologies”.
 “We cannot allow for the devastating reality of breaching 1.5C to justify overshoot scenarios that promote Carbon Dioxide Removals,” said Meena Raman of Sahabat Alam Malaysia.
 “The fantasy of removals is unproven, dangerous, and costly, and puts us all at risk. Our lives and livelihoods are at risk of being gambled on the wild dreams of the corporations and rich countries who created this crisis. Real, community-based solutions need to be put back on the table.”
 Lise Masson of Friends of the Earth International added: “The Presidency is treading a dangerous line. Climate Justice means that science and equity must go hand in hand. False solutions like Carbon Dioxide Removal promoted by rich countries, corporations, and this Presidency will push frontline communities further into climate disaster. Cop31 is increasingly at risk of sanctioning overshoot with disastrous results.”
 View image in fullscreen An activist from Fridays For Future holds a sign during a protest titled "Europe wake up!" at Cop31. Photograph: Chris McGrath/Getty Images Share Updated at  07.39 EST 3h ago 07.21 EST On methane, the strong but short-lived planet-heating gas, the draft recognises its importance for overshoot of the 1.5C target and encourages faster action in reducing its emissions – “in particular from fugitive processes” by which the oil and gas industry vents, flares or leaks large volumes of the stuff into the atmospheres.
 “We welcome the explicit call for countries to accelerate proven methane mitigation measures, strengthen emissions measurement and reporting, eliminate routine flaring and venting, and capture methane from waste,” said Jonathan Banks from the Clean Air Task Force (CATF). “These measures can deliver massive near-term climate benefits while strengthening energy security, improving air quality, and reducing wasted resources.”
 Share 3h ago 07.07 EST The first reactions to the draft cover text are already coming in to my colleague Fiona Harvey.
 “It is good to see a comprehensive draft containing ambitious language covering the key priorities, but at 144 paragraphs, it is incredibly long and the approach looks to be putting it all in and letting Parties fight for the trade-offs,” said Cosima Cassel, a climate diplomacy expert from E3G, a think tank. “The test will be whether the final decision keeps the core elements once that process plays out: ambition on overshoot, defence of the science, clean electrification and forward progress on adaptation finance.”
 Tzeporah Berman, of the Fossil Fuel Non-Prolfieration Treaty Initiative, warned that despite the reference in this draft text to the “transition away from fossil fuels”, this Cop was still likely to end without a clear promise of a phase-out.
 She told the Guardian: “There is no plan here at Cop to include phasing out fossil fuels in the agenda and there isn’t even a commitment to make a plan. This mention in the draft text will last about 2 minutes and they know it.”
 Andreas Sieber of the campaigning group 350.org told the Guardian that the Turkish and Australian co-hosts had “barely lifted a finger” to further the roadmaps to transition away from fossil fuels that some countries have urged them to take forward. “They must now secure a place for the transition in the cover decision or launch a credible political process, building on Brazil’s fossil fuel roadmaps and feeding into the next Global Stocktake.”
 He added: “You cannot claim to lead the world’s climate negotiations while refusing to lead on the transition away from fossil fuels. The credibility of both presidencies is now on the line.”
 Share 4h ago 06.55 EST Draft deal calls for 'accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels'
 Fiona Harvey A draft “cover decision” has been issued to delegates, containing some of the most contentious resolutions under discussion at this Cop.
 The text is 18 pages long and contains 144 separate items, and many of them are unlikely to survive in their current form through future drafts.
 The items include a resolution that this Cop “Calls for accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels, including through the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems.”
 Although all countries signed up to an almost exactly similar pledge in Dubai at Cop28 – though without the key word “immediate” – this resolution has never been repeated in its original form.
 Language on the “overshoot” of the 1.5C temperature goal is also included, expressing “deep concern” for the scientific findings and insufficiency of efforts to keep the target within reach, reaffirming resolve to limit the duration and magnitude of overshoot, and recognising that this will be determined by the pace and scale of climate action.
 Turkey’s priority, of a goal to derive 35% of final energy from electricity by 2035, is also in the text, with language that includes taking into account different national circumstances and accelerating the clean energy transition through increased clean electrification.
 View image in fullscreen People protest, demanding ‘Zero waste in, fossil fuels out,’ during Cop31. Photograph: Antonio Bat/EPA This draft text is only the first pass at a cover decision, which could end up being one of the main outcomes from this Cop. At this point, it is supposed to gather priorities from all countries and set out those which could make it into the final outcome.
 There are still at least four and a half days of heavy negotiating to go, so this text will go through many more iterations. And the first task for the presidency is to get agreement that a cover decision should be one of the outcomes – some countries are against even that, and are challenging the legality of having a cover decision, despite having signed up to cover decision at most of the other 30 Cops held to date.
 “This is very much to enable [negotiation] over the next week. There are elements in this draft that not all parties would agree with,” said Chris Bowen, Australia’s president of negotiations. “We believe it does provide a very good basis for conversations over the next four days.”
